newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to privatise tobacco/wine monopoly by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to privatise tobacco/wine monopoly by 2000.

text.p: Taiwan's liquor and tobacco monopoly said on Thursday it would be privatised by 2000, a market-opening move seen as improving the island's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.
"It is the government's policy to liberalise the tobacco and wine market," a Taiwan Tobacco and Wine Monopoly Bureau official said by telephone.
The official, who would not comment directly on the move's effect on Taiwan's WTO application, said the liberalisation still needed final approval from the finance ministry.
The monopoly official said Taiwan aimed to turn the bureau into a company within three years, though a controlling interest likely would remain in the state's hands after privatisation.
The United States and other WTO leaders have listed Taiwan's liquor and tobacco monopoly as a key barrier to the island's entry to the world trade body.

Analysts said the announcing of a timetable for the monopoly's privatisation during the WTO's inaugural ministerial meeting in Singapore reflected Taipei's keen desire to remove all remaining obstacles to WTO membership.
A slow liberalisation actually began in 1987, when Taiwan began allowing licensed private companies to import alcoholic beverages freely -- subject to stiff monopoly fees.
Liquor and cigarette imports, dominated by private firms, surpassed 170 million litres (45 million gallons) and 520 million packs in the fiscal year that ended in June.
The monopoly still handles most airport duty-free sales, which do not enter customs and are not counted as imports.
Monopoly fee revenues related to liquor and tobacco hit T$19.7 billion (US$716 million) in the fiscal year.
Domestic liquor and cigarette production, which remains a monopoly of the bureau, yielded T$75.5 billion in sales revenues in the fiscal year.
After liberalisation, private firms could begin producing and monopoly fees would be eliminated, with revenues replaced by standard sales and business income taxes, the official said.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade, as a customs territory under the name of Chinese Taipei.
GATT was replaced by the WTO in January 1995.
Taiwan has made major concessions in recent years in its drive to join the world trade body, allowing more imports and opening up domestic markets and dismantling state monopolies.

Rival China, which has seen Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has said it would accept Taiwan's WTO membership as a customs territory -- but only after China itself is allowed entry.
